text:
CITATION
:
Noble v. York
University Foundation, 2010 ONSC
399

COURT
FILE NO.:
07-CV-329851CM3

MOTION HEARD:
January 15, 2010

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
David
Franklin Noble, plaintiff

AND:

York University Foundation et. al., defendants

BEFORE:
Master
R.A. Muir

COUNSEL:
Y.
Hameed for the moving party/plaintiff

C. Lui, for the responding
parties/defendants York University Foundation, Paul Marcus and Lorna Marsden

REASONS FOR DECISION

[
1
]

This is a motion brought by the plaintiff
pursuant to Rules 34.12 and 34.15 of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
(the
“Rules”). The plaintiff seeks an order to compel the re-attendance of the
defendant Paul Marcus (“Marcus”), in his own capacity and in his capacity as a
representative of the defendant York University Foundation (the “Foundation”),
and the defendant Lorna Marsden (“Marsden”), to answer questions refused on
their respective examinations for discovery.

[
2
]

This is a defamation action in which the
plaintiff is claiming damages in the amount of $19,000,000.00. The plaintiff is
a professor who teaches history in the Division of Social Sciences and the
Department of Social and Political Thought at York University in Toronto. Marcus is
the President and Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation, Marsden is the
former President and Vice Chancellor of York University and a former
ex
officio
board member of the Foundation.

[
3
]

On November 15, 2004, the plaintiff prepared
what the statement of claim describes as a fact sheet entitled “The York
University Foundation – The Tail that Wags the Dog (Suggestions for Further
Research)”.

[
4
]

According to the statement of claim this
document identified connections between the Foundation and pro-Israeli
organizations and activists.

[
5
]

On November 17, 2004, the plaintiff distributed
this document during one of his lectures at York University. On November 18, 2004, the plaintiff again distributed
the document during another of his lectures at York and again on that date at a film event on the York campus.

[
6
]

The document distributed by the plaintiff in his
lectures and at the film event contained the following statements, among
others:

(a)

the Foundation “is the tail that wags the dog that is York University”;

(b)

the Foundation “is biased by the presence and influence of staunch
pro-Israel lobbyists, activists and fundraising agencies”; and,

(c)

certain decisions of Marsden and the Board of Directors “appear to
reflect the strongly pro-Israel orientation of the [Foundation]”.

[
7
]

In response to the distribution of this
document, York University and
the Foundation issued a press release on November 19, 2004 in which they
condemned this “highly offensive material, which singles out certain members of
the York community on the basis
of their ethnicity and alleged political views”. In the press release, this
statement is attributed to Marsden.

[
8
]

In his statement of claim the plaintiff alleges
that this press release and Marsden’s statements, and a subsequent email,
regarding the flyer distributed by the plaintiff were defamatory.

[
9
]

The plaintiff also alleges that Marcus was
involved in “planning the content and dissemination of the defamatory email on
behalf of the Foundation”. It is not clear from the statement of claim what
particular email the plaintiff is referring to when he makes this allegation.

[
10
]

As a result of these allegedly defamatory
statements (and others attributed to the other defendants to this action
arising out of the same events), the plaintiff alleges that his “professional
reputation and the pursuit of his trade or calling as a University Professor
has been disparaged and seriously and irrevocably harmed”.

[
11
]

On December 6, 2007, the Foundation, Marsden and
Marcus delivered their statement of defence in which they deny the plaintiff’s
allegations. Of particular importance to this motion are paragraphs 7 to 9 of
the statement of defence which read as follows:

7.

In the Flyer, the plaintiff falsely asserted,
inter
alia
, that:

(a)

The Foundation “is the tail that wags the dog that is York University”;

(b)

The Foundation “is biased by the presence and influence of staunch
pro-Israel lobbyists, activists and fundraising agencies”; and,

(c)

Certain decisions of Marsden and Board of Directors “appear to
reflect the strongly pro-Israel orientation of the [Foundation]”.

8.

In listing in his flyer, without any further
support, 11 of the 24 members of the Board of Directors of the Foundation who
are Jewish persons or who are affiliated with Jewish person or organizations,
the plaintiff asserted or inferred that such members of the Foundation are
pro-Israel lobbyists, and through them, the Foundation effectively controlled
the University.

9.

These defendants were concerned with the
contents of the Flyer, especially as it appeared to attribute impropriety to
certain persons who are members of the Board of Directors of the Foundation
and, in particular, that such persons are pro-Israel lobbyists controlling the
University.

[
12
]

Marcus and Marsden were examined for discovery
on May 27, 2008. At page 35, question 144 of Marsden’s examination she was
asked the following question:

Q.        And can you say whether some - - or I guess some or many
of the individuals [listed in the flyer], whether they are pro-Israel
lobbyists, activists or fundraising agencies?

A.        Don’t answer that. We’ve been through that issue once
today already. That’s not a proper question. Asking whether or not someone is
pro-Israel is like asking if someone is pro-American. You can be pro-American
and have differing views on all kinds of issues. It isn’t a black and white
matter. So I don’t think that’s a proper question and I’m not going to allow
it.

[
13
]

At page 48, question 120 of Marcus’ examination,
he was asked the following question:

Q.        . . . I’m wondering if you can identify which, if any, of
the board members listed here would be pro-Israeli in their political
orientation, and I’ll be more specific about the question, that’s to say with
respect to the dispute in Israel-Palestine whether these individuals would have
a proclivity one way or another, whether you would call them pro-Israeli or
pro-Palestinian?

A.        Don’t answer that. I don’t think that’s a question that’s
capable of being answered in such simplistic terms. I don’t think this witness
could possibly know what is in the minds of other people and I think that the
question couldn’t be answered in the way that you’ve framed it in any event.

[
14
]

In deciding the issues on this motion I have
applied the relevance test set out in Rule 31.06(1), as amended effective
January 1, 2010. This test replaces the “semblance of relevance” test
previously applicable to motions such as this. While the examinations of
Marsden and Marcus took place in May, 2008 and this motion was scheduled in
December, 2009, it was not heard until January 15, 2010 after the Rules
amendments came into force. The January 1, 2010 Rules amendments do not contain
any transition provisions relating to the change from “semblance of relevance”
to “relevance”. Consequently, it is my view that the “relevance” test is
applicable to this motion. This is also the view taken by Justice Belobaba in
Onex
Corp. v. American Home Assurance,

2009 CanLII 72052 (ON SC)
, [2009] O.J. No. 5526 (S.C.J.) in relation
to the Rules amendments dealing with summary judgment.

[
15
]

In applying the relevance test I am mindful of
the comments found in the
Summary of Findings and Recommendations of the
Civil Justice Reform Project
led by the Honourable Coulter A. Osborne, upon
which the January 1, 2010 Rules amendments are based. In particular I note the comments
at part 8 of the Report dealing with discovery:

I agree with these
views. The “semblance of relevance” test ought to be replaced with a stricter
test of “relevance.” This step is needed to provide a clear signal to the
profession that restraint should be exercised in the discovery process and, as
the Discovery Task Force put it, to “strengthen the objective that discovery be
conducted with due regard to cost and efficiency.” In keeping with the
principle of proportionality, the time has come for this change to be made,
which I hope in turn will inform the culture of litigation in the province,
particularly in larger cities.

This reform is
not targeted at lawyers who make reasonable discovery requests, but rather at
those who make excessive requests or otherwise abuse the discovery process.
Therefore, a change from “relating to” to “relevant” would likely have little
or no impact on those lawyers who already act reasonably during the discovery
process. Its effects will be felt by those who abuse discovery or engage in
areas of inquiry that could not reasonably be considered necessary, even though
they currently survive “semblance of relevance” analysis.

[
16
]

At paragraph 7 of their statement of defence,
the defendants Marsden, Marcus and the Foundation state quite clearly that the
plaintiff’s allegation in his flyer that the Foundation “is biased by the
presence and influence of staunch pro-Israel lobbyists, activists and
fundraising agencies”, is false. At paragraph 9 of their statement of defence,
the defendants Marsden, Marcus and the Foundation state that they were concerned
with the contents of the plaintiff’s flyer insofar as it appeared to suggest
that the directors of the Foundation listed in the flyer were “pro-Israel
lobbyists controlling the University”.

[
17
]

It is well settled law that the pleadings
determine whether a particular question is relevant and must be answered.  On
discovery, the plaintiff is entitled to test the statements made by Marsden,
Marcus and the Foundation in their pleading. They have stated that the
plaintiff’s allegations about the Foundation are false. The plaintiff is
entitled to know what evidence each of them may have in relation to that
statement. Subsequent to the scheduling of this motion, both Marsden and Marcus
agreed to answer the plaintiff’s questions about whether they personally are “pro-Israel”.
Presumably because they now agree that those questions are relevant. If these
defendants are going to take the position that the plaintiff’s allegations
about the Foundation’s directors are false, they must answer the plaintiff’s
questions about what they know about the relevant beliefs and activities of the
directors.

[
18
]

In my view the questions asked by the plaintiff
of Marsden and Marcus, set out above, are directly relevant to issues raised by
those defendants in their pleading and should be answered. The questions more
than meet the standard of relevance established by Rule 31.06(1).

[
19
]

The plaintiff has also asked that the court
order Marsden and Marcus to re-attend at an examination to provide those
answers. In my view this request is premature. There is no automatic right to
require re-attendance to obtain answers to undertakings or questions improperly
refused where it serves no useful purpose. See
Senechal v. Muskoka
(Municipality)
,
2005 CanLII 11575 (ON SC)
, [2005] O.J. No. 1406 (S.C.J. – Master) at paragraph
7
. This
is not a situation where there are numerous questions to be answered. The
re-attendance requested here relates to only two related questions to each
witness. Given this, and the fact that we do not yet know what their answers
will be, I decline to exercise my discretion to order re-attendance at this
time.

[
20
]

Following the completion of argument, the
parties exchanged costs outlines and provided copies to the court. I have
considered the factors and principles set out in Rules 1.04(1.1), 57.01(1) and
57.03(1). I have also reviewed and considered the costs outlines of each of the
parties.

[
21
]

The plaintiff was largely successful on this
motion other than his request for an order for re-attendance. His full
indemnity costs total $8,744.77 including disbursements. His substantial
indemnity costs are $6,995.82 including disbursements. His costs outline does
not indicate an amount for partial indemnity costs. The hours spent in
preparing for and attending on this motion appear reasonable given the work
involved (motion materials, factum, legal research and attendance). However, I
do not see any basis for an award of costs on a substantial indemnity scale.
Therefore, taking into account the plaintiff’s lack of success on the
re-attendance issue, I have concluded that the defendants Marsden, Marcus and
the Foundation shall pay the plaintiff’s costs of this motion fixed in the
amount of $4,000.00 inclusive of disbursements and GST, payable within 30 days
of the date of these reasons for decision.

[
22
]

The court therefore orders:

(a)

Marcus shall, on his own behalf and on behalf of the Foundation,
answer the question posed to him at page 48, question 120 of his examination
for discovery within 30 days;

(b)

Marsden shall answer the question posed to her at page 35, question
144 of her examination for discovery within 30 days;

(c)

Marsden, Marcus and the Foundation shall pay to the plaintiff his
costs of this motion, fixed in the amount of $4,000.00, inclusive of
disbursements and GST, within 30 days of the date of these reasons for
decision.

Master R. A. Muir

Date: February 17, 2010
